photo.caption: Swirling patterns of a massive phytoplankton bloom in the North Sea, captured by NASA's Terra satellite on June 6, 2015. Though microscopic, phytoplankton blooms can span vast areas and play a crucial role in marine food webs and the global carbon cycle.
photo.alt: The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) flying aboard NASA s Terra satellite flew over the North Sea on June 6, 2015 and captured this beautiful true-color image of a spring phytoplankton bloom in progress.
photo.description: Sometimes the view from space can lend credence to ancient myths, such the mythic tales of sea serpents thrashing in the waters of the North Sea, between the British Isles and Norway. In early June, 2015, a massive phytoplankton produced sinuous swirls of color reminiscent of a creature swimming in the sea, recalling stories such as the Norse Jormungand, a fearsome sea serpent which was said to be cast into the sea by Odin, eons ago. Also known as the Midgard Serpent, the beast was said to be a mortal enemy of Thor, the stormy protector of mank

photo.fileTitle: File:NASA satellite view of Southern Ocean phytoplankton bloom (crop).jpg
photo.caption: NASA satellite view of Southern Ocean phytoplankton bloom
photo.description: NASA satellite view of Southern Ocean phytoplankton bloom On January 13, 2016, the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi NPP satellite captured this view of extensive phytoplankton blooms stretching from the tip of South America across to the Antarctic Peninsula. The image was built with data from the red, green, and blue wavelength bands on VIIRS, plus chlorophyll data. A series of image-processing steps highlighted the color differences and more subtle features, such as nearly a dozen eddies of varying sizes.

photo.caption: Vertical transport of carbon in the ocean. POC aggregates sink through the water column leading to remineralization and long-term carbon storage.
photo.description: Components of the biological pump Photic zone: 0–100 m; Mesopelagic: 100–1000 m; Bathypelagic: 1000 to abyssal depths. Below 1000 m depth carbon is considered removed from the atmosphere for at least 100 years. Scavenging: DOC incorporation within sinking particles.

photo.caption: Overview of the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage. (A). The phage binds to the surface of a bacterial cell. (B) Genetic material is injected into the host. (C) The host's machinery is hijacked to reproduce viral DNA. (D). Bacteriophages build up until the intracellular contents burst, releasing the virus to be taken up again.
photo.description: Illustrative representation of the bacteriophage lytic cycle. A) The phage has binding proteins (illustrated as pink spheres) that recognize specific membrane receptors (red receptors) on the target bacterium. B) Upon receptor-ligand recognition, the bacteriophage adheres to the bacterium's membrane and then releases its genetic material. C) The genetic material introduced into the cell is recognized by bacterial proteins, which transcribe and translate the viral genes, leading to the synthesis of new bacteriophages. photo.description: Mature biofilm structure Biofilm is characterized by heterogenous environment and the presence of a variety of subpopulations.
